# Building an Autonomous 24/7 AI On-Call Engineer

**Source:** https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeHphfnxfZg/ · **Type:** Reel · **Author:** Thomas Kim · **Saved:** 2026-10-12

## Summary

Episode 4 of the 10x AI-Native Developer series outlines an automated pipeline for triaging and patching production errors without human intervention. Errors caught by observability tools trigger cloud coding agents to reproduce, fix, verify, and peer-review code across multiple LLMs before merging.

## Transcript and on-screen text

How To Become a 10x AI-Native Developer Ep. 4 of 7
I created a 24/7 AI on call engineer that fixes errors and bugs for me while I sleep, and I want to show you how it works. This is episode 4 of 7 in my How To Become A 10X AI Native Developer series, and in the first three videos, I talked about the importance of creating verification skills so that your models know how to use your application. And when you pair these verification skills with cloud coding agents, this becomes even more powerful because now the cloud coding agents can actually go write code, verify and validate that it works, and merge it without you being involved in the entire process. And this is actually a great pattern that you can use to create an on call engineer that fixes errors for you autonomously so that you can focus on the product work and not the annoying error and bug fixes. So first, you need to have some type of service that will capture errors within your app. This video is not sponsored by anyone at all, and for me, I use PostHog. Whenever PostHog captures an error, it sends it over to my error fix bot right here, and this is essentially the starting point for my 24/7 AI on call engineer. It'll receive the error, and then what it'll do is it'll kick off a cloud coding agent from within Cursor, and then within every single cloud coding agent, it follows a very precise process. Number one, verify that it can reproduce the original error itself on its own computing environment. And only once the cloud coding agent can verify that the error is reproducible in its own local dev environment, it'll then create a fix, verify it works using the actual production data that it used to reproduce the original bug, and verify that the code changes it makes actually works using the verification skills that I talked about in episode one of this series. And then once it's able to verify the fix actually works and fixes the original error, it then determines how big or how small of a risk it is to merge this without me being involved. The general principle that it follows is if it's just a small, one-off bug fix, go ahead and merge it without me. If it's a larger architectural change to fix a larger widespread bug, it does not merge on its own, and instead, it asks it to actually request a review from me first before merging it. And then lastly, before that actually gets merged, it actually gets reviewed by other models as well. So within Cursor cloud coding agents, I use Grok 4.7 to actually do the implementation, then I force the code that Grok 4.7 wrote to get reviewed by both GPT 6.1 as well as Opus 5.5, and only when all three models say that the code is safe to merge, then does a merge on its own. ## Caption
